newsitem.title: INDIA: India's rulers, Congress lock hands for presidency.
newsitem.headline: India's rulers, Congress lock hands for presidency.

text.p: Flanked by both the prime minister and Congress party leader, Vice President Kocheril Raman Narayanan registered on Friday to run for India's president in a show of unusual political solidarity.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Congress president Sitaram Kesri were joined by at least five cabinet ministers as Narayanan filed his nomination papers for the indirect election set for July 14.

The presence of leaders from Gujral's United Front coalition and Congress lent an aura of invincibility to Narayanan, a journalist-turned-diplomat and former Congress minister who is all but assured of becoming India's first low-caste president.
Wary of each other in many areas, the United Front and Congress amiably joined hands this week to back the vice president.
Under the Indian parliamentary system, the president is the titular head of state and has few real powers compared to the prime minister, who is the head of government.
But the constitution empowers the president to pick the prime minister.
In the past 13 months after inconclusive general elections, President Shankar Dayal Sharma has had to name three prime ministers at the head of coalition governments.
"I am privileged to be the joint nominee of the Congress and United Front in the election," Narayanan said.
With their backing, Narayanan is virtually assured of winning the election, which will involve voting by members of the federal parliament and the assemblies in the 26 states.

The main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has not yet endorsed a candidate. Its ruling partner in Maharashtra state, the Shiv Sena, has thrown its support behind the outspoken former election commissioner, T.N. Seshan.
Since India became a republic in 1950, the presidency has been held by 10 presidents who were either upper-caste Hindus, a Sikh and two Moslems.
